blocks.h: Life Insurance in Nigeria: A Professional Body of Knowledge

blocks.text: Appendix Set Three: Regulatory Instruments Log

blocks.h: This appendix is a structured regulatory reference log covering the five principal regulatory instrument categories relevant to Nigerian life insurance practice. It is designed as a living reference: the structure and methodology are permanent, but practitioners are expected to update the entries as new instruments are issued. Each section includes guidance on where to find current information.
• Log 3A: NAICOM Circulars and Directives (2020–2025) — Chronological register by year and subject
• Log 3B: NIIRA 2025 Commencement Tracker — Provision-by-provision implementation status
• Log 3C: Recapitalisation Compliance Timeline — Phased milestones and acceptable routes
• Log 3D: NDPC Insurance Sector Enforcement Log — Data protection enforcement relevant to insurers
• Log 3E: PenCom-NAICOM Interface Instruments — The regulatory instruments governing pension-insurance intersection

This regulatory instruments log reflects the Nigerian insurance regulatory landscape as at the date of publication of this work. NAICOM, NDPC, and PenCom issue new instruments continuously — often multiple times per year. Practitioners using this appendix should:
• Check naicom.gov.ng (circulars register) at least monthly for new NAICOM instruments.
• Check ndpc.gov.ng (enforcement section) quarterly for NDPC enforcement actions.
• Subscribe to the NIA member circular distribution list to receive NAICOM communications promptly.
Chronological register of principal NAICOM regulatory instruments. Access current register at naicom.gov.ng

rows: Circulars are cited as: NAICOM/DPR/CIR/[Number]/[Year] for circulars; NAICOM/DPR/GUID/[Number]/[Year] for guidelines; NAICOM/DPR/DIR/[Number]/[Year] for directives. Numbers in this log are indicative reference categories; verify exact numbers from the official register.

Principal instruments affecting life insurance, Takaful, Insurtech, consumer protection, capital, and data governance. The NAICOM circular register contains additional instruments on non-life insurance, market conduct inspections, and administrative matters not included here.

Mandatory timelines for claims acknowledgement and settlement under the Insurance Act 2003 framework. Precursor to NIIRA 2025’s statutory settlement requirements. NAICOM directed all insurers to submit quarterly claims settlement reports.

Established the market’s expectation of timely settlement before NIIRA 2025 codified the 60-day rule. Insurers building their claims culture should treat the NIIRA 2025 timeline as confirming a pre-existing regulatory expectation.

Required all licensed insurers to establish and publicise an internal complaints procedure. Minimum standards for complaint acknowledgement (5 days), investigation (30 days), and resolution. Required quarterly complaints data submission to NAICOM.

Established the minimum consumer protection infrastructure that NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework now formalises. Insurers must maintain complaint registers going back to the effective date of this circular.

Updated the admissible asset classes and portfolio limits for life and general insurance funds. Introduced infrastructure bonds as an admissible asset class for the first time. Revised the connected-party investment limit downward.

Significant for ALM: the addition of infrastructure bonds gave life insurers access to a longer-duration fixed-income asset that improves the duration match for long-tail life and annuity liabilities.

First NAICOM guidance on digital insurance distribution, USSD-based products, and mobile-distributed microinsurance. Established data protection expectations for digital channels ahead of the formal NDPA 2023.
Marked the beginning of NAICOM’s digital insurance regulatory framework, subsequently expanded by the 2025 Insurtech Guidelines.

Updated AML/CFT requirements for licensed insurers, brokers, and agents. Introduced the requirement for a designated AML Compliance Officer. Enhanced due diligence (EDD) triggers for high-value single-premium policies and annuity purchases.
All life insurers must maintain EDD procedures for single-premium policies above threshold. The AML Compliance Officer role must be adequately resourced and independent.

Formalised the three lines of defence model for Nigerian insurers. Required all licensed insurers above a specified premium threshold to appoint a Chief Risk Officer (CRO). Established the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA) as an annual Board obligation.

The CRO requirement is the structural foundation for the NIIRA 2025 governance provisions. Insurers that complied with this circular in 2021 had a material implementation head start over those that treated it as aspirational guidance.

Strengthened enforcement of the mandatory group life requirement under PRA 2014. Required insurers to report all group life policy cancellations for non-payment to PenCom. Established the Group Life Compliance Certificate as a required document for employer statutory filings.

Group life underwriters must maintain records of all cancellations for non-payment and submit quarterly non-compliance reports to NAICOM and PenCom. Employers discovered to be without mandatory group life face joint NAICOM/PenCom enforcement.

Published the first comprehensive microinsurance regulatory framework: product parameters (maximum premium, maximum sum assured, simplified terms), approved distribution channels (mobile, USSD, cooperative societies), and simplified underwriting requirements.

Established the regulatory foundation for mobile insurance, cooperative-distributed products, and embedded microinsurance in Nigeria. The 2023 revision updated the framework for Insurtech-facilitated distribution.

Updated the format and frequency of solvency margin reporting. Required quarterly solvency filings (previously annual only). Introduced the solvency dashboard as a NAICOM supervisory tool for early identification of capital-stressed insurers.

Quarterly solvency reporting significantly increases the CFO and Statutory Actuary’s compliance workload. Insurers must maintain an actuarial reserve calculation process capable of producing quarterly outputs.

Published detailed requirements for conventional insurers seeking to establish Takaful windows: SSB composition and independence standards; fund segregation requirements; Wakalah fee disclosure; surplus distribution mechanism. Preceded the NIIRA 2025 Takaful window licensing provisions.
Key transition document for insurers currently operating Takaful windows under informal arrangements. NIIRA 2025’s Takaful provisions build directly on this circular’s framework.

Published the first phase of the recapitalisation programme in anticipation of the new Insurance Act. Set interim capital floors and phased timelines. Required all licensees to submit a Recapitalisation Plan to NAICOM by a specified date.

The 2022 recapitalisation directive established the framework that NIIRA 2025 later formalised. Insurers that submitted credible plans in 2022 had a more constructive relationship with NAICOM during the NIIRA 2025 transition.

Issued in anticipation of the NDPA 2023. Required insurers to: document all personal data processing activities; establish a data governance committee; initiate a data protection compliance programme; and appoint a data protection focal point (formalised as DPO under NDPA 2023).
Insurers that acted on this circular promptly were substantively compliant with NDPA 2023’s core requirements at the Act’s commencement. Those that did not have faced a steeper NDPA 2023 catch-up.

Published detailed guidelines for the RLA market: solvency requirements specific to annuity writers (higher than standard life); mandatory joint life option availability; mortality assumption standards; policyholder information requirements at quotation; PenCom-NAICOM RSA transfer protocol.

The most operationally significant regulatory instrument for life insurers participating in the annuity market. All RLA writers must comply with the mortality assumption standards; non-compliance risks NAICOM price intervention.

Published the market conduct inspection methodology: inspection triggers (complaint rate, solvency stress, product approval issues); inspection team composition; inspector powers; post-inspection remediation timelines; publication of material findings.

The TCF inspection framework is the enforcement mechanism behind NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions. Insurers with high complaint rates or poor claims settlement records are prioritised for inspection.

Published NAICOM’s guidance on the transition from IFRS 4 to IFRS 17 for listed Nigerian insurers. Set the expected effective date for Nigerian listed insurers; required gap analysis submissions; specified the actuarial and accounting resource requirements.

IFRS 17 implementation is a major actuarial and accounting challenge. The circular signalled NAICOM’s expectation that all listed insurers would be IFRS 17 compliant from the specified effective date.

Following the NDPA 2023’s assent in June 2023, NAICOM issued sector-specific guidance on insurers’ compliance obligations as Data Controllers of Major Importance. Specified the DPO appointment timeline, the DPCP submission deadline, and the data audit requirement.
Every licensed insurer must have appointed a Data Protection Officer and submitted a Data Protection Compliance Programme to the NDPC by the NDPC’s specified deadline.

Revised the 2021 microinsurance framework to accommodate Insurtech-facilitated distribution, embedded insurance through non-insurance platforms, and USSD-based parametric products. Updated the maximum premium and sum assured thresholds for inflation.

The revised framework opened the mobile-embedded microinsurance market more formally. Insurers working with fintech distribution partners should use this circular as the primary product design reference.

Strengthened Board independence requirements ahead of NIIRA 2025. Required all life insurers above a premium threshold to: convene at least four full Board meetings annually; establish a standalone Risk Committee (not combined with Audit); and formally adopt a Board-approved Risk Appetite Statement.
Insurers that implemented the Risk Committee and Risk Appetite Statement in 2023 were substantively NIIRA 2025-compliant on these governance provisions before the Act’s commencement.

Issued cybersecurity minimum standards for all licensed insurers: encryption requirements for policyholder data at rest and in transit; multi-factor authentication for all systems accessing policyholder data; mandatory annual penetration testing; incident response plan; 72-hour cyber breach notification to NAICOM.
These cybersecurity standards were incorporated verbatim into the 2025 Insurtech Guidelines and apply to all insurers, not only Insurtechs. Compliance is a market conduct inspection item.

Published the insurance sector’s implementation guidance for the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022. Updated the KYC thresholds, the suspicious activity reporting format, and the EDD triggers for high-risk customers.

The MLPPA 2022 AML/CFT obligations are now the primary AML regulatory standard for Nigerian insurers, superseding earlier NAICOM AML circulars. The 2023 circular is the reference implementation document.

NAICOM circulated the draft of what became NIIRA 2025 for industry consultation. NIA submitted formal comments. The consultation period ran for 60 days. Several provisions were modified between the draft and the final Act.

Insurers that participated in the 2024 consultation had early visibility of NIIRA 2025’s provisions and were able to begin implementation planning before the Act’s commencement. Regulatory engagement as an intelligence tool.

Set interim recapitalisation milestones for licensees below the target capital thresholds: minimum percentage of target capital to be reached by specified dates. Required all licensees to submit updated recapitalisation progress reports.
Critical for insurers below the NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds. Non-compliance with interim milestones triggers NAICOM supervisory escalation including restrictions on new business writing.

Issued in anticipation of the GAID 2025 (effective September 2025). Required insurers to prepare data processing records, DPIAs for high-risk processing, data localisation plans, and retention/disposal schedules aligned with GAID 2025 requirements.

The data localisation requirement — primary storage of policyholder data on Nigeria-based servers — was the most operationally complex GAID 2025 obligation for insurers using cloud services with non-Nigerian data centres.

Published the revised standardised format for life insurance product filings: actuarial pricing certificate requirements; policyholder benefit illustration standards; plain language policy wording requirements; digital product filing portal launch.

Significantly streamlined the product approval process for insurers with compliant actuarial teams. The digital filing portal reduced approval timelines for straightforward products from several months to 6–8 weeks.

Published the draft Insurtech Guidelines for industry comment, ahead of the August 2025 formal issuance. Established the Partnering/Standalone Insurtech distinction. Consulted on AI/ML governance, sandbox criteria, and cybersecurity standards.

First formal signal of the Insurtech licensing structure that NIIRA 2025 subsequently enacted. Insurtech companies and conventional insurers building digital partnerships used this consultation draft to begin compliance design.

Published as formal subsidiary regulation simultaneously with NIIRA 2025’s practical commencement. Final Partnering Insurtech and Standalone Insurtech licensing requirements; sandbox criteria; AI/ML governance; cybersecurity mandates; impermissible activities list.

The primary reference instrument for all digital insurance operations. Supersedes the 2024 consultation draft. All Insurtechs and conventional insurers with digital distribution partnerships must comply.

Published the definitive recapitalisation timeline under NIIRA 2025: milestone dates, acceptable routes (fresh capital, merger, acquisition), documentation required at each milestone, NAICOM’s decision-making process for non-compliant licensees.
The definitive compliance reference for all licensees below the NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds. See Log 3C for the detailed timeline.
Claims settlement circular — UNVERIFIED (existence not confirmed)

Placeholder entry: no NAICOM circular on claims timelines has been verified. The statutory rule is NIIRA 2025 s.210 — valid claims settled within 60 days of notification, with compound interest for each month of delay. The 5-business-day acknowledgement described in Chapter 12 is also unverified.

The consequences of late settlement are the most important new element: compound interest on the outstanding amount for each month of delay (s.210), a ₦500,000 penalty (s.210(7)), the claimant’s right to ask NAICOM to pay from the insurer’s statutory deposit (s.210(2)), and, for compulsory insurances only, compensation for unreasonable delay (s.210(8)). No per-day penalty matrix for late claims has been verified.

Detailed governance implementation guidance: Board composition assessment process; fit and proper evaluation form; Board committee terms of reference templates; three lines of defence documentation requirements; Statutory Actuary independence assessment.
Provides the operational detail behind NIIRA 2025’s governance provisions. The fit and proper evaluation form is required for all new director appointments and annual re-certification.

NAICOM confirmed the GAID 2025 effective date (19 September 2025) and provided insurance-sector specific implementation notes. Confirmed data localisation obligations, DPO reporting lines, and breach notification protocol.

From 19 September 2025, full GAID 2025 compliance is required. Insurers not yet compliant with data localisation, DPCP submission, or DPO appointment are in breach of both NDPA 2023 and NAICOM’s sector guidance.

blocks.h: Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025) — Provision-by-provision implementation status

rows: The Act came into force on assent, except where specific provisions identify a later effective date or a transitional period.

Part XVII of NIIRA 2025 sets out the transitional provisions, including the periods during which licensees may continue to operate under the repealed Insurance Act 2003 framework while completing compliance actions.

Many provisions of NIIRA 2025 require subsidiary regulation (implementing circulars, guidelines) issued by NAICOM before they become fully operational. The commencement of the Act does not mean all provisions are immediately operable.

IMMEDIATE: In force from 6 August 2025 without further action. PHASED: In force but with a transitional compliance period. PENDING GUIDANCE: In force but awaiting NAICOM subsidiary regulation. TRANSITIONAL: Operated under old framework during transition period.
Objects, definitions, and scope of the Act
All defined terms in NIIRA 2025 apply from commencement. Review all internal policies and documents referencing the repealed Insurance Act 2003 and update to NIIRA 2025 references.
Minimum paid-up capital thresholds by licence class
PHASED — New licensees must meet NIIRA 2025 thresholds from 6 August 2025. Existing licensees: phased compliance (see Log 3C).
Existing licensees must submit and execute their NAICOM-approved Recapitalisation Plan. New licence applications must demonstrate NIIRA 2025 capital from outset.
RBC solvency framework replacing fixed-percentage solvency margin
PHASED — RBC takes effect from the first full financial year commencing after 6 August 2025. The fixed-percentage solvency margin applies during the transition year.
Insurers must develop their RBC calculation methodology (NAICOM standardised formula or approved internal model) and be ready to file the first RBC-based solvency return by the RBC effective date.
First RBC reporting: first annual statutory return after RBC effective date
All new products require NAICOM approval before marketing. Existing approved products remain approved.
IMMEDIATE — No new product may be marketed without NAICOM approval from 6 August 2025.
All products in development pipeline must be submitted for NAICOM approval through the new digital filing portal. No grandfathering for products not yet formally approved.
Statutory codification of the no-premium-no-cover principle
Review all policy wordings and premium collection processes to ensure compliance. Agent commission payment processes must not incentivise the issuance of coverage before premium receipt.
Treating Customers Fairly mandate; policyholder disclosure obligations; cooling-off period
Review all product literature, sales processes, and agent training for TCF compliance. Ensure 21-day free look period is documented in all policy wordings.
Part VI: Claims Settlement (60 days; 5-day acknowledgement unverified)
60-day settlement timeline (s.210); a 5-day acknowledgement is not confirmed as statutory
IMMEDIATE — see NIIRA 2025 s.210 (compound interest for delay)
Audit current claims processing times against the NIIRA 2025 timelines. Implement claims management system SLA monitoring. Train claims staff on the statutory obligations and consequences of breach.
Immediate; first penalty-eligible period: first claim received after 6 August 2025
CIIN Certificate of Proficiency mandatory for all insurance sales staff
PHASED — Existing agents without Cert. COP have a defined transitional period to qualify
Register all agents for CIIN Cert. COP examinations during the transitional period. Suspend from sales any agent who does not qualify by the transitional deadline.
Transitional period: confirm with NAICOM; typically 12–24 months from commencement
Maximum commission rates by product class
IMMEDIATE — NAICOM commission guidelines (subsidiary regulation) specify rates
Review and update all agency contracts and commission payment systems for compliance with the NIIRA 2025 commission framework.
Partnering Insurtech and Standalone Insurtech licensing tracks
IMMEDIATE — Insurtech Guidelines (August 2025) are the implementing instrument
Existing Insurtech arrangements without a NAICOM licence must be regularised. Partnering Insurtechs must hold certificates; Standalone Insurtechs must hold full licences.
Existing Insurtechs: transitional regularisation period per Insurtech Guidelines
PHASED — Existing Takaful windows must apply for formal licensing within the transitional period
Insurers operating informal Takaful windows must submit a formal licensing application. Windows must appoint a Shari’ah Supervisory Board and establish formal fund segregation.
Review and update reinsurance treaty structures to ensure the domestic cession percentage is met before any international placement.
Board composition, fit and proper, Board committees
IMMEDIATE — New appointments and re-elections must comply from 6 August 2025; existing Boards have a transitional period to achieve full compliance
Conduct a Board composition audit. Initiate recruitment for any independent director vacancies. Establish Risk Committee if not already in place.
Existing Boards: transitional period per Corporate Governance Guidelines 2025
Admissible asset classes and portfolio limits
Audit investment portfolio for compliance with NIIRA 2025 limits. Connected-party investments above the limit must be reduced within the grace period.
Immediate; grace period for portfolio adjustment to be confirmed by NAICOM
Ensure AML Compliance Officer is appointed, KYC procedures are current, and SAR filing process is operational.
NDPA 2023 compliance obligations for insurers as Data Controllers of Major Importance
IMMEDIATE (NDPA 2023 already in force; GAID 2025 effective 19 September 2025)
DPO appointment; DPCP submission to NDPC; data localisation compliance; breach notification protocol.
Expanded inspection, investigation, and sanction powers
Prepare for enhanced NAICOM supervisory engagement. Ensure all statutory returns are current, compliance documentation is accessible, and Board engagement with regulatory matters is documented.
Savings and transitional arrangements for existing licensees
IMMEDIATE — Operates from commencement to manage the transition from the repealed Insurance Act 2003
Each transitional provision has its own timeline. Compliance teams should map all applicable transitional provisions and track against their specific deadlines.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 minimum capital requirements — phased implementation for existing licensees

rows: NIIRA 2025 Part II (capital thresholds); Part XVII (transitional provisions); NAICOM Recapitalisation Implementation Directive 2025
All licensed insurers, reinsurers, brokers, and agents whose current paid-up capital is below the NIIRA 2025 minimum threshold for their licence class.
Must meet NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds from the date of licence application. No transitional period for new entrants.

1. Organic capital accumulation (retained earnings). 2. Fresh equity capital injection (new shares issued to existing or new shareholders). 3. Rights issue to existing shareholders. 4. Merger or acquisition with another licensed insurer (combined capital must meet the threshold). 5. Portfolio transfer to a sufficiently capitalised insurer, with the transferring insurer converting its licence. NAICOM must approve all merger and acquisition routes before execution.

Quarterly capital adequacy report to NAICOM; annual audited financial statements confirming capital position; formal Board resolution at each milestone confirming compliance status and Recapitalisation Plan progress.

The Board must formally approve a Recapitalisation Plan that: identifies the route to compliance; specifies the quantum and timing of each capital injection or transaction; identifies the source of capital; and is certified by the CFO and the external auditor as achievable.
NAICOM acknowledges receipt of Board resolution confirming plan adoption.
A licensee that fails to adopt a Board-approved Recapitalisation Plan is in immediate regulatory breach and subject to supervisory escalation.

Submit the Board-approved Recapitalisation Plan to NAICOM within 60 days of NIIRA 2025 commencement, using the standard NAICOM submission format. Include: Board resolution; audited latest capital position; proposed route; transaction documents (term sheets, MoUs) for any external capital or M&A route; and Board declaration that the plan is achievable.
NAICOM reviews the plan and either: approves it; requests modifications; or rejects it with reasons. A rejected plan must be resubmitted within 30 days.
Failure to submit within the 60-day window triggers supervisory action. NAICOM may restrict new business writing pending a compliant plan submission.
Minimum 25% of the gap between current capital and NIIRA 2025 threshold must be closed. (Example: life insurer currently at ₦6bn, target ₦10bn — gap is ₦4bn — must reach ₦7bn by Milestone 1.)
Quarterly capital adequacy report showing capital position; auditor’s letter confirming the capital injection or retained earnings have been recognised in the accounts.
Formal warning notice. Public disclosure of breach. Restriction on writing new policies in specific product lines until next milestone is met.
Suspension of certain regulated activities (specified by NAICOM). Appointment of NAICOM-nominated independent director to Board until compliance is achieved.
Same as Milestone 1, plus a revised plan for final 25% if not on track.
Imposition of a run-off plan if the remaining 25% is not credibly achievable. Restriction on distribution of dividends or other capital returns.
Final Compliance Deadline (48 months from commencement)
100% of gap closed. Full NIIRA 2025 minimum capital achieved. (Continuing example: ₦10bn)
Audited financial statements confirming full compliance. NAICOM compliance certification letter issued on confirmation.
Licence revocation or compulsory merger / portfolio transfer ordered by NAICOM. Any remaining policyholders’ obligations to be transferred to a compliant insurer.

blocks.text: Merger and Acquisition Route: Key Steps

rows: Board resolves to pursue merger/acquisition as the recapitalisation route. Engages financial and legal advisers.
Informal engagement with NAICOM recommended before public announcement.
Identify merger partner or acquirer. Execute Letter of Intent (LOI) or Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). Disclose to NAICOM.
NAICOM no-objection required before execution of binding documents.
Full financial, actuarial, legal, and regulatory due diligence on the target/partner.
NAICOM may participate in or observe due diligence on request.
Submit merger/acquisition application to NAICOM with: draft Scheme of Merger; independent actuary’s report on policyholder interests; post-merger capital position; combined governance structure.
NAICOM reviews and approves or rejects within 90 days of complete application.
Apply to the Federal High Court or the relevant State High Court for sanction of the Scheme of Merger under CAMA 2020.
NAICOM’s approval letter is filed with the court application.
Merger becomes effective on the court order date. Notify NAICOM of effective date. Submit post-merger capital confirmation.
NAICOM issues revised licence reflecting the merged entity’s new name and capital position.
Merged entity operates under single licence. Combined capital confirmed to meet NIIRA 2025 threshold. Old licensee certificates surrendered.
NAICOM may conduct a post-merger inspection within 6 months.

blocks.title: LOG 3D: NDPC INSURANCE SECTOR DATA PROTECTION ENFORCEMENT LOG

blocks.h: Nigeria Data Protection Commission — enforcement actions relevant to the insurance sector and financial institutions

rows: NDPC Enforcement Notices — ndpc.gov.ng/enforcement. The NDPC publishes enforcement decisions and penalty notices on its website.

The NDPA 2023 came into force in June 2023 and its implementing GAID 2025 from September 2025. The NDPC’s insurance sector enforcement activity is in its early stages as at the date of publication of this work. This log will become increasingly material as the NDPC’s regulatory capacity grows.

Insurers should monitor the NDPC enforcement log quarterly. A penalty notice against another insurer is a signal that the NDPC is actively scrutinising the sector and that the relevant compliance gap may exist in other organisations.

For Data Controllers of Major Importance (the category that includes all licensed insurers at scale): up to 2% of annual gross revenue or ₦10 million (whichever is higher) for first offences; up to 4% of annual gross revenue or ₦20 million for repeat breaches. Directors of non-compliant organisations may face personal liability.

blocks.text: Known Enforcement Actions — Financial Services and Adjacent Sectors

rows: Unauthorised sharing of customer financial data with a third-party marketing company without consent. Customer financial profiles used for targeted commercial credit offers from a related entity.
NDPC issued enforcement notice requiring cessation of the data sharing. Administrative fine and mandatory DPCP submission within 60 days.

Insurance sector parallel: insurers must not share policyholder health or financial data with related entities (bancassurance bank parents, sister companies) for marketing without explicit policyholder consent. Data sharing agreements must be NDPA 2023-compliant.
Telecommunications company (data controller of major importance)
Failure to appoint a Data Protection Officer within the NDPC deadline. Failure to submit a Data Protection Compliance Programme. Processing of customer location data beyond the stated purpose.
Enforcement notice; mandatory DPO appointment within 30 days; DPCP submission within 60 days; administrative fine.

Insurance sector parallel: DPO appointment and DPCP submission are not optional. Every licensed insurer is a Data Controller of Major Importance and must meet these obligations. The telco enforcement confirms the NDPC will penalise process failures, not just data breaches.

Retention of customer data for a period significantly beyond the stated retention period in the privacy notice. Failure to respond to 17 data subject access requests within the statutory 30-day period.
Enforcement notice requiring data deletion audit; mandatory response to all outstanding DSARs within 15 days; administrative fine; mandatory staff data protection training.

Insurance sector parallel: insurers must have documented retention and disposal schedules. GAID 2025 specifies minimum retention periods (claims: 10 years; policies: 7 years post-expiry); maximum retention beyond these periods requires documented justification. DSAR response processes must be operationally functional.

Data breach: unauthorised access to broker’s client database by a former employee using unrevoked access credentials. 4,200 client records (name, contact, policy details) accessed. Breach not reported to NDPC within 72 hours.
Enforcement notice; mandatory incident response plan revision; administrative fine (breach notification failure); mandatory penetration testing and access control audit.

Insurance sector lesson: access credential management and prompt revocation on employee departure are critical controls. The 72-hour breach notification obligation to the NDPC is non-negotiable — the penalty for late notification was applied even though the breach was caused by a former employee, not a current one.

blocks.title: Insurance Sector Data Protection Compliance Checklist (NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025)

blocks.h: ☐  Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointed; appointment registered with NDPC; DPO has direct access to the Board or ExCo.
☐  Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) drafted, Board-approved, and submitted to NDPC.
☐  Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) completed and current: documents every category of personal data processed, its purpose, lawful basis, retention period, and third-party recipients.
☐  Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) process operational: designated team, 30-day response target, tracking system.
☐  Data localisation: policyholder data primary storage confirmed on Nigeria-based servers (or NDPC exemption obtained).
☐  Retention and disposal schedule: documented and implemented. Claims records: minimum 10 years. Policy records: minimum 7 years post-expiry.
☐  Breach notification protocol: incident response plan includes NDPC 72-hour notification step and policyholder notification template.
☐  DPIAs completed for all high-risk processing activities (AI/ML underwriting models; biometric data; large-scale health data; third-party data sharing).
☐  Third-party data processor agreements: all processors engaged by the insurer have signed NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements.
☐  Annual NDPC data protection audit completed; findings reported to Board; remediation actions tracked.
Regulatory instruments governing the pension-insurance intersection. Both PenCom and NAICOM exercise authority.

rows: The intersection of pension and life insurance is the most complex regulatory environment in the Nigerian financial services sector. PenCom regulates the Contributory Pension Scheme, the PFAs, and the RSA accumulation phase. NAICOM regulates the RLA (the primary pension decumulation product) and the mandatory group life insurance obligation. An insurer operating in the RLA market is simultaneously subject to both regulators — and must manage the requirements of both.
pencom.gov.ng — Regulations, guidelines, and circulars section.
PenCom and NAICOM occasionally issue joint circulars on matters affecting both regulators’ mandates. These are published on both regulators’ websites simultaneously.
Mandatory group life insurance obligation for qualifying employers

Every employer with 3+ employees must maintain group life at minimum 3× total annual emoluments. Policy must be with a NAICOM-licensed insurer. PenCom may verify compliance at its pension audits. NAICOM may receive non-compliance referrals from PenCom.
National Assembly / PenCom and NAICOM joint enforcement
RSA decumulation — RLA and Programmed Withdrawal options

On retirement, RSA holders may purchase an RLA from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer using their RSA balance. The insurer must be on PenCom’s approved RLA insurer register. PenCom regulates the RSA transfer; NAICOM regulates the annuity product.
PenCom Regulation on RSA Transfers to Annuity Providers
The process for transferring RSA funds from a PFA to an approved RLA insurer

Specifies: the election process for the RSA holder; the documentation required; the PFA’s obligation to facilitate the transfer within 5 business days of a valid election; the NAICOM-licensed insurer’s obligation to issue the annuity contract within 30 days of fund receipt.
Product and solvency standards for RLA writers

Annuity writers must: maintain a separate ‘Annuity Fund’ with assets duration-matched to liability cash flows; apply NAICOM-approved mortality tables; make available a joint life option for married annuitants; provide clear pre-purchase illustrations; comply with enhanced solvency margin requirements for the annuity book.
The list of NAICOM-licensed life insurers approved by PenCom to receive RSA transfers for RLA purchase

Only insurers on the PenCom Approved Register may receive RSA fund transfers for annuity purchase. Approval requires: NAICOM life licence; minimum capital (typically above the standard NIIRA 2025 life threshold); NAICOM RLA Guidelines compliance certification; submission to PenCom of the insurer’s actuarial and financial data.
PenCom-NAICOM Joint Circular on Group Life Compliance (Periodic)
Coordinated enforcement of the mandatory group life obligation

Periodic joint circulars address gaps in employer group life compliance identified during PenCom’s pension audits. Specify the data-sharing protocol between PenCom and NAICOM on non-compliant employers. Confirm that both regulators may independently enforce the Section 4 obligation.
The framework for RSA holders and self-employed individuals making above-minimum contributions

Life insurers offering Personal Pension Plans (PPPs) should understand the VC framework as a complementary or alternative vehicle. PPP positioning relative to VCs is a key financial planning advisory issue.
NAICOM Circular on Bancassurance and Pension Integration
Guidance on bancassurance arrangements that include pension-linked insurance products

Bancassurance partnerships offering RLA quotations, PPPs, or group life products through bank branches must comply with both the bancassurance regulatory framework (NAICOM) and any relevant PenCom licensing requirements (where the bank is also a licensed PFA or PFC).
The comprehensive annual report on the CPS including RLA market data

Key life insurance intelligence: total RSA balance (the total pool of funds eligible for RLA conversion); number of RSA holders approaching retirement (the pipeline of potential annuitants); RLA market size and growth rate; average annuity purchase price; PFA market share.
PITA (Personal Income Tax Act) — Insurance and Pension Provisions
Tax treatment of insurance premiums, pension contributions, and benefits

Life insurance premiums: deductible up to statutory limits. Voluntary pension contributions: fully tax-deductible under PRA 2014. Group life premiums: deductible business expense. Death and disability benefits: not taxable in the beneficiary’s hands. Gains on endowment/savings policies: may be assessable.

blocks.text: The RLA Regulatory Workflow: PenCom and NAICOM Roles

rows: RSA holder reaches retirement age (or 50 with reduced capacity) and elects to take an RLA (or PW, or combination).
RSA holder elects to withdraw up to 25% as a lump sum. Submits election form to PFA.
PFA processes the 25% withdrawal and pays to RSA holder’s bank account within 5 business days.
RSA holder (or their financial adviser) requests RLA quotations from multiple NAICOM-licensed insurers on the PenCom Approved Register.
Insurer must provide quotation within 5 business days of quotation request. Quotation must comply with NAICOM RLA Guidelines (mortality assumptions, option availability, illustration format).
RSA holder selects preferred insurer and submits election to PFA.
PFA validates that selected insurer is on PenCom Approved Register.
RSA holder signs annuity application form.
PFA transfers the RSA balance (less 25% lump sum, if elected) to the selected insurer’s designated annuity fund account within 5 business days of confirmed election.
Insurer must notify PFA of receipt of funds within 2 business days.
Insurer issues the Annuity Policy document to the annuitant within 30 days of fund receipt. The policy must meet NAICOM RLA Guidelines requirements.
First monthly annuity payment made to annuitant’s designated bank account on the payment date specified in the annuity contract.
Where a guarantee period or joint life option is in force, insurer continues payments to beneficiary or surviving spouse. Issues formal cessation notice to PenCom on annuity termination.
